comments.author: @p-51d95
comments.text: In the last few days I've heard "Jevon's paradox" more times than I can count. Here is the possible issue... it is not that there will not be more demand for GPUs, it's when that demand will occur. Even with a 10x reduction in training and inference the demand will occur. And it will be huge, but only once applications are developed to take advantage of it. In the meantime it is conceivable that Nvidia chips are no longer the bottleneck and this could have a big impact on margins. Nvidia is not going away. It will still sell lots of chips but when and at what margin. A similar thing happened early in the development of the internet when a lot of long-haul optical fiber links were laid. Eventually all this fiber was used (Jevon's paradox) but it was only when a number of internet apps (eg streaming video,  etc) were built that required it. For a number of years during the early days of the internet this fiber remained dark. The question is whether this analogy holds this time. History doesn't repeat but it does sometimes rhyme.

comments.author: @clivefoo
comments.text: The hype in AI can sometimes feel like the emperor’s new clothes—buzzwords, overblown promises, or exaggerated capabilities can create an illusion of groundbreaking advancements, even when the actual substance may not measure up. However, just as in the story, there are often those who point out the gaps or limitations. The challenge lies in distinguishing genuine innovation from empty hype, as the true value of AI lies in its practical, impactful applications—not just the spectacle. When billions are being pumped in, the pressure to deliver, or at least appear to deliver, can lead to a cycle of overpromises. Investors chase the “next big thing,” and startups or companies might exaggerate capabilities to secure funding. This creates an ecosystem where hype sometimes overshadows real progress, and the “new clothes” are sold before they even exist. It’s not to say there isn’t meaningful work being done, but the gap between marketing and reality can grow wider when so much money is at stake.
